newsitem.title: JAPAN: Asian Metals - Japan's copper market remains quiet.
newsitem.headline: Asian Metals - Japan's copper market remains quiet.

text.p: The physical copper market in Japan is quiet, ignoring a price surge in the London Metal Exchange (LME) copper market, traders said on Wednesday.
LME benchmark three-month copper prices rallied on Tuesday to a six-month high of $2,285 a tonne before drifting back to $2,258, up $54 from Monday.
That was the highest level since mid-June when Sumitomo Corp shocked the copper world by firing its former star trader Yasuo Hamanaka and blaming him for massive trading losses.
Recent rallies have been spurred by drawdowns in LME warehouse stocks, which dipped on Tuesday to a 6-1/4 year low of 90,050 tonnes.
"There's surely a growing supply tightness in Europe and North America, and the situation is likely to remain at least until next month," a copper trader at a major trade house said.
"But we don't see such tightness in Asia," he said.
Japanese traders believe some foreign brokers still hold copper positions, which were built up by Hamanaka and were transferred to them by Sumitomo Corp later.
Sumitomo said last week that it retains some copper positions related to the trading losses, but it does not expect any further upward revisions to its estimated losses of $2.6 billion.

"In the process of liquidating the positions, Sumitomo might have transferred some to other brokers. That means Hamanaka's copper positions remain somewhere in the market," another copper trader said.
The recent surge in LME aluminium prices has not tempted Japanese end-users to alter their hand-to-mouth buying, but some are expected to start buying in the spot market next month, traders said.
"Some Japanese firms failed in their timing to buy aluminium ahead of the recent price rallies. They may now have to buy by the end of this year," an aluminium trader said.
Japanese trade houses and end-users are continuing premium negotiations with foreign suppliers for the first quarter of 1997, traders said.
"While the Japanese side wants to set the premiums at about $60, sellers hope to raise them to $65. We expect a conclusion by next week," another aluminium trader said.
The premiums for the October-December period of this year were set at about $62 per tonne over LME cash prices.
